title: The utility and relative cost of using detection dogs compared to traditional methods for surveying small, cryptic mammals: A case study on the threatened Julia Creek dunnart, Sminthopsis douglasi
content:
by Emma L. Gray, Amanda Hancock, Ayesha Tulloch, Andrew M. Baker

Accurate population monitoring is required to ensure timely conservation. However, it is often difficult to detect species that occur at low densities using traditional live-trapping survey methods, especially if they are small and/or cryptic. Here, we assessed the utility and cost efficiency of detection dogs as a rapid detection strategy by modelling a threatened Australian dasyurid marsupial, the Julia Creek dunnart (Sminthopsis douglasi). The detection dogs were systematically trained to discriminate the odour of S. douglasi from co-occurring small mammals and were able to detect the target species under controlled and natural field conditions. Compared to live-trapping surveys, detection dogs had a higher upfront cost but became more cost-effective after multiple surveys due to much quicker time to first indication/capture and survey duration times. When we predicted the costs of undertaking surveys according to the Australian Government survey guidelines for S. douglasi our research suggested that detection dogs were clearly more cost-efficient under paid labour scenarios when moderate-large areas required survey. In contrast, for a low number of surveys, small assessment areas, or where surveys could be undertaken with unpaid volunteers, traditional live-trapping surveys were the most affordable method to detect S. douglasi. However, a major limitation of the detection dog surveys was the difficulty in corroborating dog indications with a secondary detection method. Due to our inability to rule out potential false positive errors for uncorroborated indications, we recommend that all uncorroborated indications be considered ‘probable records’. We propose that future detection dog surveys for S. douglasi (and similar taxa) incorporate a set of criteria to grade confidence in indications when secondary corroboration is not logistically feasible or achievable. Final choice of detection method will therefore depend on the budget and purpose of the surveys, the size of the area and/or the number of surveys required.
